questions.stem: How does the combined oral contraceptive pill mainly prevent pregnancy?
options: Its hormones suppress FSH and LH, so ovulation does not occur
It kills sperm in the vagina before they can reach the cervix
It forms a physical barrier that covers the cervix during intercourse
It blocks the oviducts so that the egg cannot reach the uterus
questions.explanation: The synthetic steroid hormones exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so no LH surge occurs and no egg is released. Killing sperm is the action of spermicides.

questions.stem: A woman using fertility awareness charts her body temperature each morning. Why does she look for a small, sustained rise?
options: It shows that ovulation has already occurred in that cycle
It shows that ovulation will occur in about a week's time
It shows that menstruation has just ended
It shows that she is pregnant from that cycle
questions.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum raises resting body temperature slightly after ovulation. Because the rise only confirms ovulation has passed, it cannot warn of the fertile days before it.

questions.stem: Why is fertility awareness less reliable for people with irregular cycles?
options: Irregular cycles mean no ovulation occurs, so the charts give false readings
Body temperature does not change at all in women with irregular cycles
Irregular cycles make sperm live much longer in the female tract
Ovulation is harder to predict, and sperm can survive for days before it
questions.explanation: Abstaining at the right time depends on predicting ovulation several days ahead, because sperm already present can fertilise the egg. With irregular cycles that prediction is much less certain.

questions.stem: Which contraceptive method also gives good protection against most sexually transmitted infections?
options: The combined pill
A hormonal implant
A vasectomy
Condoms
questions.explanation: Condoms are a physical barrier that stops semen and vaginal fluids passing between partners, so they reduce STI transmission as well as pregnancy. Hormonal methods and sterilisation give no STI protection.

questions.stem: How does a diaphragm work as a contraceptive?
options: It kills sperm in the testes before ejaculation
It covers the cervix, keeping sperm out of the uterus
It releases hormones that stop the ovaries releasing eggs
It is placed in the oviduct and blocks the egg's path
questions.explanation: A diaphragm is a flexible dome placed over the cervix before intercourse, usually with a spermicide, physically keeping sperm out of the uterus.

questions.stem: Spermicides are rarely recommended on their own. Why?
options: They permanently damage the lining of the uterus
They work only if taken by mouth every day
Used alone they fail more often than most other methods
They stop ovulation for several months after a single use
questions.explanation: Spermicides chemically immobilise or kill sperm, but not every sperm is reached, so they are much more effective combined with a barrier such as a diaphragm or condom.

questions.stem: Which statement about tubal ligation is correct?
options: The ovaries are removed, so no eggs or hormones are produced
The uterus is removed, so menstruation stops immediately
The cervix is sealed, so it is very easily reversed later
The oviducts are cut or blocked, so sperm and egg cannot meet
questions.explanation: Tubal ligation blocks the oviducts; the ovaries keep releasing eggs and hormones and menstruation continues. It is intended to be permanent.

questions.stem: After a vasectomy, a man is advised to use other contraception until a semen test shows no sperm. Why?
options: Sperm already beyond the cut can still be ejaculated for some time
The testes keep producing sperm that leak through the cut vas deferens
Testosterone levels rise after the operation, which increases fertility
The vas deferens always rejoins within a few weeks of the operation
questions.explanation: A vasectomy stops new sperm reaching the urethra, but sperm stored further along the tract remain for a number of ejaculations. A semen test confirms they have cleared.

questions.stem: How does the emergency contraceptive pill mainly work when taken soon after unprotected sex?
options: It permanently prevents ovulation for the rest of the woman's life
It delays ovulation, so it is most effective the sooner it is taken
It ends an established pregnancy by detaching the embryo from the uterus
It kills sperm already in the oviduct within minutes of being taken
questions.explanation: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation so sperm present cannot meet an egg; they are less effective with each day of delay and do not end an established pregnancy.

questions.stem: A copper intrauterine device (IUD) can be used as emergency contraception if inserted within a few days of unprotected sex. How does it prevent pregnancy?
options: Copper is absorbed into the blood and suppresses the release of FSH and LH
The device blocks the oviducts so the egg cannot be released from the ovary
The device releases oestrogen that thickens the endometrium for many years
Copper is toxic to sperm and the device hinders implantation
questions.explanation: Copper ions impair sperm and the device causes changes in the uterine lining that hinder implantation. Hormonal IUDs release a progestogen instead.

questions.stem: A contraceptive implant placed under the skin of the arm releases a progestogen. Which is an advantage and which a limitation?
options: Advantage: permanent and cannot be reversed. Limitation: stops menstruation forever
Advantage: has no effect on hormones at all. Limitation: must be used with spermicide
Advantage: works for years without daily action. Limitation: no protection from STIs
Advantage: protects against all STIs. Limitation: must be replaced every day
questions.explanation: Long-acting reversible methods such as implants are highly effective because they don't rely on daily use, and fertility returns after removal. Like all hormonal methods, they do not prevent STIs.

questions.stem: Chlamydia often causes no symptoms. Why is this a concern for women?
options: It means the infection is passed only to men and never to a newborn baby
Untreated infection can spread and scar the oviducts, causing infertility
It means the infection cannot be treated once it is finally detected
It means the infection is caused by a virus that antibiotics cannot kill
questions.explanation: Chlamydia is a bacterial infection that is easily cured with antibiotics, but undetected it can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and scarring of the oviducts, leading to infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which sexually transmitted infection is caused by a virus?
options: Genital herpes
Chlamydia
Gonorrhoea
Syphilis infection
questions.explanation: Genital herpes is caused by herpes simplex virus and has no cure, though antiviral drugs reduce outbreaks. Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis are bacterial and treated with antibiotics.

questions.stem: How does HIV damage the body's ability to fight infections?
options: It blocks the lymph vessels, so tissue fluid cannot be returned
It infects the bone marrow, so no platelets can be produced
It destroys helper T cells, weakening the immune response
It destroys red blood cells, so tissues receive too little oxygen
questions.explanation: HIV targets helper T lymphocytes, which coordinate immune responses; as their numbers fall, opportunistic infections take hold (AIDS). Antiretroviral drugs control the virus but do not cure it.

questions.stem: How is infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) linked to cancer, and how can it be prevented?
options: Some HPV types cause cervical cancer; vaccination prevents infection
HPV causes breast cancer; regular antibiotics prevent the infection taking hold
HPV causes prostate cancer; a blood test before puberty prevents the infection
HPV causes leukaemia; avoiding sunlight prevents the virus from spreading
questions.explanation: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types causes almost all cervical cancers and some other cancers. Vaccination, ideally before sexual activity begins, prevents infection with the main types.

questions.stem: If untreated, syphilis passes through several stages over many years. Why is early detection important?
options: Early stages can only be treated by surgery, which is not possible in the later stages
Early detection allows the virus to be removed before it enters the nervous system
Early detection prevents the infection spreading only to the person's lymph nodes
Early stages are cured with antibiotics, preventing later damage to the brain and heart
questions.explanation: Syphilis is a bacterial infection curable with penicillin; if untreated it can spread and cause serious damage to the nervous system, heart and other organs, and can be passed to a foetus.

questions.stem: Gonorrhoea is becoming harder to treat in some places. Why?
options: Strains of the bacterium have become resistant to many antibiotics
The virus mutates too quickly for antiviral drugs to work
It now spreads only through the air, so condoms no longer help
It has become a fungal infection that no medicine can now reach
questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium that has developed resistance to several antibiotics, which is why testing, completing treatment and safe sex are emphasised.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes in vitro fertilisation (IVF)?
options: Hormones stimulate the ovaries, eggs are collected and fertilised in the lab, and an embryo is transferred
Sperm are placed directly into the uterus at ovulation, and fertilisation occurs in the oviduct as usual
Eggs are collected and frozen, then returned to the ovary so they can be released at the next ovulation
An embryo is collected from the uterus of one woman and grown to term in a laboratory incubator
questions.explanation: IVF uses fertility drugs to mature several eggs, collects them, fertilises them outside the body and transfers an embryo to the uterus a few days later. Placing sperm into the uterus is artificial insemination.

questions.stem: A couple's infertility is caused by the man having very few, poorly motile sperm. Which technology is most suitable?
options: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) of one sperm into an egg
Tubal ligation, cutting the oviducts to stop eggs being released
A hormonal implant, slowly releasing progestogen to improve the sperm
Amniocentesis, sampling fluid to find which eggs are healthy
questions.explanation: In ICSI a single sperm is injected directly into each egg, so fertilisation does not depend on sperm swimming or penetrating the egg. It is used as part of IVF.

questions.stem: Why do many clinics now transfer only one embryo at a time in IVF?
options: To increase the cost so that fewer people choose to use IVF
To reduce multiple pregnancies, which carry higher risks
Because a second embryo always destroys the first in the uterus
Because only one egg can ever be collected during each IVF cycle
questions.explanation: Transferring several embryos raises the chance of twins or triplets, with greater risks of premature birth and pregnancy complications. Spare embryos can be frozen for later use.

questions.stem: Which is a recognised risk of the hormone treatment used in IVF?
options: Ovarian hyperstimulation, when the ovaries over-respond
Permanent loss of all eggs from the ovaries within one cycle
Infection of the embryo with HIV from the culture medium
Fusion of two embryos into one with four sets of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Fertility drugs can over-stimulate the ovaries, causing swelling, fluid retention and pain, which is occasionally serious. Doses are monitored to reduce this risk.

questions.stem: An IVF embryo has a few cells removed for genetic testing before transfer. Which ethical concern is most often raised about this?
options: The test changes the embryo's DNA, so the child is no longer genetically its parents' own
The test gives the embryo a disease that it did not have before sampling
Embryos may be chosen for traits other than disease, and unused embryos discarded
The test always harms the embryo so badly that it cannot develop normally
questions.explanation: Pre-implantation genetic testing lets parents avoid serious inherited disorders, but raises questions about selecting embryos for non-medical traits and the fate of embryos not chosen.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares chorionic villus sampling (CVS) and amniocentesis?
options: CVS samples the mother's blood and carries no risk at all to the pregnancy
Amniocentesis samples the embryo's brain tissue to check for brain defects
CVS samples placental tissue and can be done earlier than amniocentesis
Amniocentesis samples placental tissue and is done earlier in pregnancy than CVS
questions.explanation: CVS takes cells from the chorionic villi of the placenta, usually in the first trimester; amniocentesis withdraws amniotic fluid containing foetal cells later. Both carry a small risk of miscarriage.

questions.stem: How can cells obtained by amniocentesis be used to detect Down syndrome?
options: The cells are counted to see whether the foetus is growing at all
The fluid is cultured for bacteria to see if the foetus has an infection
Foetal cells are cultured and their chromosomes examined in a karyotype
The fluid's sugar level is measured to see if the foetus is diabetic
questions.explanation: The fluid contains cells shed by the foetus; their chromosomes can be arranged as a karyotype, revealing an extra chromosome 21. DNA tests on these cells can also detect single-gene disorders.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has a blood test that analyses foetal DNA fragments in her blood and returns a high-risk result for trisomy 21. What should happen next?
options: A diagnostic test such as CVS or amniocentesis is offered
The result is treated as certain and no further testing is needed
The test is repeated every day until the result changes to low risk
An ultrasound is used to correct the foetus's extra chromosome
questions.explanation: Blood tests of this kind are screening tests that estimate risk; a high-risk result needs confirming by a diagnostic test on foetal or placental cells. No test can correct a chromosome abnormality.

questions.stem: Why is ultrasound widely used to monitor a pregnancy?
options: It shows foetal growth and structure without invasive sampling
It reads the foetus's DNA sequence to find all inherited disorders
It collects foetal cells from the amniotic fluid for a karyotype
It uses X-rays to give clear pictures of the foetal skeleton
questions.explanation: Ultrasound uses reflected high-frequency sound to image the foetus, checking age, growth, number of foetuses and many structural abnormalities, with no known risk from routine use. It does not analyse DNA.

questions.stem: What does the cervical screening test look for?
options: Lumps in the breast tissue too small to feel by hand
Raised levels of a protein released by the prostate
Infection with high-risk types of HPV
Antibodies showing that the woman has been vaccinated
questions.explanation: The cervical screening test detects HPV, which causes almost all cervical cancers, so people at risk can be followed up before cancer develops. The older Pap test looked only for abnormal cells.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of breast screening with mammograms?
options: Testing breast milk for viruses passed to a baby when feeding
Measuring hormone levels to predict the date of menopause
Finding breast cancers early, often before a lump can be felt
Preventing breast cancer by destroying abnormal cells with X-rays
questions.explanation: A mammogram is a low-dose X-ray of the breast that can detect small cancers early, when treatment is more likely to succeed. Screening detects cancer; it does not prevent or treat it.

questions.stem: A man's blood test shows a raised level of prostate-specific antigen (PSA). Why does this not prove he has prostate cancer?
options: PSA falls when cancer is present, so a raised level rules it out
PSA is a hormone that every man produces at the same level
PSA also rises with non-cancerous prostate enlargement or infection
PSA is produced only by the testes, not by prostate tissue at all
questions.explanation: PSA is made by prostate tissue and rises in cancer, but also with benign enlargement and inflammation, so a raised result usually leads to further tests such as imaging or a biopsy.

questions.stem: Why is pregnant women's alcohol intake a concern for the foetus?
options: Alcohol crosses the placenta and can damage the developing brain
Alcohol is filtered out by the placenta, but it reduces the mother's appetite
Alcohol only affects the foetus after it is born and starts breastfeeding
Alcohol changes the sex of the foetus if drunk in the first trimester
questions.explanation: Alcohol passes freely across the placenta and can cause foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), with lifelong effects on learning and behaviour. Not drinking during pregnancy is the safest choice.

questions.stem: How does smoking during pregnancy reduce the growth of the foetus?
options: Tar coats the umbilical cord so that no nutrients can pass along it
Carbon monoxide lowers blood oxygen and nicotine narrows blood vessels
Nicotine increases blood flow to the placenta, so the foetus is overfed
Smoke particles travel through the placenta and block the foetal lungs
questions.explanation: Less oxygen in the mother's blood and narrowed vessels reduce the supply to the foetus, increasing the risk of low birth weight and premature birth.

questions.stem: Why are women advised to take folic acid (folate) before conception and in early pregnancy?
options: It prevents the foetus from developing Down syndrome
It stops the mother's blood from clotting during birth
It increases the number of eggs released each cycle
It lowers the risk of neural tube defects
questions.explanation: Adequate folate while the neural tube forms, in the first weeks after conception, reduces neural tube defects. It cannot prevent chromosomal conditions such as Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Why are the first eight weeks after fertilisation the period when the embryo is most vulnerable to harm from drugs and alcohol?
options: This is when the major organs and body systems are forming
This is when the foetus gains most of its body mass
This is when the placenta filters out all harmful substances
This is when the foetal skeleton becomes fully hardened bone
questions.explanation: During the embryonic period cells are differentiating to form the organs, so interference can cause major structural defects. Most growth in mass happens later, in the foetal period.

questions.stem: A baby born to a mother who regularly used opioids during pregnancy shows withdrawal symptoms such as tremors and poor feeding. What explains this?
options: The drug changed the baby's blood group so it reacts to the mother's milk
The baby caught an infection from the drug that causes these symptoms
The drug crossed the placenta, and the supply stopped suddenly at birth
The baby inherited an allele for opioid use from its mother's chromosomes
questions.explanation: Many illicit drugs cross the placenta, so the foetus becomes dependent; once the supply stops at birth, the newborn shows withdrawal (neonatal abstinence syndrome).

questions.stem: Contraception and assisted reproduction both raise ethical questions. Which question is an ethical one rather than a scientific one?
options: Should unwanted frozen embryos be donated, used for research or discarded?
How many embryos usually develop to blastocysts after fertilisation in a laboratory?
How much does a progestogen implant lower the levels of LH in a woman's blood?
At what temperature must embryos be stored to remain viable for later transfer?
questions.explanation: Ethical questions ask what ought to be done and depend on values, such as the status of embryos and consent. The other questions can be answered by measurement and experiment.

questions.stem: Which contraceptive method is a form of sterilisation in males?
options: Vasectomy
Diaphragm
Spermicide
Fertility awareness
questions.explanation: A vasectomy cuts or seals each vas deferens so sperm cannot enter the semen; it is intended to be permanent. The other methods are temporary.

questions.stem: What is a sexually transmitted infection (STI)?
options: A disorder of the reproductive hormones that begins at puberty
An infection that can only be caught from contaminated food
An infection passed on through unprotected sex or genital contact
An inherited disorder passed from parents to children in their genes
questions.explanation: STIs are caused by bacteria, viruses or other pathogens spread through sexual contact. Safe sex, testing and early treatment reduce their spread and their long-term harm.

questions.stem: Which technique places prepared sperm directly into the uterus around the time of ovulation?
options: Artificial insemination
In vitro fertilisation
Amniocentesis
Tubal ligation
questions.explanation: In artificial (intrauterine) insemination, sperm are placed in the uterus so fertilisation can occur naturally in the oviduct. In IVF, fertilisation happens outside the body.
